Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

This article gives the proof of results announced in [J. Blanc, Finite Abelian subgroups of the Cremona group of the plane, C.R. Acad. Sci. Paris, S\'er. I 344 (2007), 21-26.] and some description of automorphisms of rational surfaces.   Given a finite Abelian subgroup of the Cremona group of the plane, we provide a way to decide whether it is birationally conjugate to a group of automorphisms of a minimal surface.   In particular, we prove that a finite cyclic group of birational transformations of the plane is linearisable if and only if none of its non-trivial elements fix a curve of positive genus. For finite Abelian groups, there exists only one surprising exception, a group isomorphic to Z/2ZxZ/4Z, whose non-trivial elements do not fix a curve of positive genus but which is not conjugate to a group of automorphisms of a minimal rational surface.   We also give some descriptions of automorphisms (not necessarily of finite order) of del Pezzo surfaces and conic bundles.

The article establishes results previously announced by J. Blanc and gives a detailed description of automorphisms of rational surfaces. In particular, it develops a method for deciding whether a finite Abelian subgroup of the plane Cremona group is birationally conjugate to a group of automorphisms of a minimal rational surface.

A central result concerns finite cyclic groups of birational transformations of the plane: such a group is linearisable—that is, birationally conjugate to a group of projective linear transformations—if and only if none of its non-trivial elements fixes a curve of positive genus. For finite Abelian groups, this fixed-curve criterion has a unique exception. The group
\[
\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}\times \mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z}
\]
satisfies the condition that none of its non-trivial elements fixes a curve of positive genus, yet it is not birationally conjugate to an automorphism group of any minimal rational surface.

The article also provides a broader study of automorphisms of rational surfaces, including automorphisms of both finite and infinite order. Particular attention is given to the two principal classes of minimal rational surfaces arising in this setting: del Pezzo surfaces and conic bundles.
outputs.L4:
The article studies finite Abelian subgroups of the plane Cremona group
\[
\operatorname{Cr}_2(\mathbb C)=\operatorname{Bir}(\mathbb P^2),
\]
with particular emphasis on the problem of birational conjugacy. Given such a group \(G\), one asks whether a birational change of coordinates transforms its action on the projective plane into a biregular action on a minimal rational surface and, ultimately, whether it is conjugate to a subgroup of \(\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbb P^2)=\operatorname{PGL}_3(\mathbb C)\). Groups with the latter property are called linearisable.

After resolving the indeterminacies of the action and applying the equivariant minimal model program, every finite group action on a rational surface can be represented by a \(G\)-minimal pair \((S,G)\). The resulting surface \(S\) is of one of two basic types: either it is a del Pezzo surface, whose anticanonical divisor is ample, or it carries a \(G\)-equivariant conic bundle structure. Thus, the conjugacy problem in the Cremona group is reduced to the study of finite Abelian groups acting biregularly on these two classes of rational surfaces.

The article develops practical criteria for determining when such an action can be birationally simplified. It examines the automorphism groups of del Pezzo surfaces of the various possible degrees and analyses the way Abelian subgroups act on exceptional curves, anticanonical systems, and other distinguished configurations. In the conic-bundle case, it studies both the action induced on the base and the subgroup acting fibrewise, paying special attention to singular fibres and to the curves fixed by nontrivial automorphisms. These descriptions make it possible to decide when a \(G\)-minimal action is genuinely non-linear and when equivariant birational transformations reduce it to an action on the projective plane or another standard rational surface.

A central birational invariant in this analysis is the existence of a curve of positive genus fixed pointwise by an element of the group. Such a curve cannot disappear under birational conjugacy: its birational type is preserved when the action is transferred to another smooth model. On the other hand, a nontrivial linear automorphism of \(\mathbb P^2\) fixes only points and rational curves. Consequently, if some nonidentity element of a finite subgroup of the Cremona group fixes a curve of positive genus, the subgroup cannot be linearisable.

For finite cyclic groups, the article proves that this necessary condition is also sufficient. More precisely, a finite cyclic subgroup \(G\subset \operatorname{Cr}_2(\mathbb C)\) is birationally conjugate to a subgroup of \(\operatorname{PGL}_3(\mathbb C)\) if and only if no nontrivial element of \(G\) fixes a curve of positive genus. This gives an intrinsic geometric characterisation of linearisable cyclic actions and unifies the treatment of cyclic automorphisms arising from del Pezzo surfaces and conic bundles.

The situation for general finite Abelian groups is slightly more subtle. In nearly every case, the same fixed-curve criterion continues to distinguish linear actions from non-linear ones. There is, however, one exceptional group:
\[
\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z\times \mathbb Z/4\mathbb Z.
\]
The article constructs and analyses a non-linearisable Cremona action of this group for which no nontrivial element fixes a curve of positive genus. Thus, although each individual element passes the cyclic linearisability test, the group action as a whole is not birationally conjugate to a linear action. The obstruction in this case is therefore genuinely collective and cannot be detected solely by examining the fixed curves of separate group elements.

This exceptional example shows both the strength and the limitation of the fixed-curve method. For cyclic groups it provides a complete criterion, whereas for finite Abelian groups one must also account for the way the elements interact within a common action. Together with the classification of Abelian actions on del Pezzo surfaces and conic bundles, the result gives a broad description of when finite Abelian subgroups of the plane Cremona group can be regularised and when they can be birationally conjugated to linear automorphisms of the projective plane.

**This Blanc Finite**

At the edge of the winter fields stood a house called Blanc, its walls as pale as untouched snow. No one remembered who had named it, only that travelers felt strangely peaceful when they saw it glowing beneath the moon.

Inside, every clock had stopped. Time seemed finite there—not frighteningly so, but gently, like the final page of a beloved book.

“This is enough,” whispered the last visitor as dawn entered through the windows.

And for the first time in many years, the clocks began to move.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an abstract for a research paper on finite Abelian subgroups of the plane Cremona group, including criteria for linearisation and results on automorphisms of rational surfaces.
counterfactuals.output: We study finite Abelian subgroups of the plane Cremona group \(\mathrm{Cr}_2(\mathbf{k})=\operatorname{Bir}(\mathbf{P}^2_{\mathbf{k}})\) over an algebraically closed field of characteristic \(0\). Using equivariant resolution of singularities and the \(G\)-equivariant minimal model program, every such subgroup is realised as a group of automorphisms of a smooth rational \(G\)-minimal surface, which is either a del Pezzo surface or a conic bundle. We give criteria for the action to be linearizable—that is, birationally conjugate to a subgroup of \(\operatorname{PGL}_3(\mathbf{k})\)—in terms of fixed points, invariant curves, and the geometry of the corresponding minimal model. We then analyse finite Abelian automorphism groups of rational surfaces, describing the restrictions imposed by the Picard lattice, singular fibres, and anticanonical geometry. This yields a classification of the non-linearizable cases and identifies the geometric and cohomological obstructions to linearisation. As applications, we obtain conjugacy results for finite Abelian subgroups of \(\mathrm{Cr}_2(\mathbf{k})\) and explicit descriptions of their regular models on del Pezzo surfaces and rational conic bundles.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the main results of Jérémy Blanc’s work on finite Abelian subgroups of the Cremona group of the plane.
counterfactuals.output:
Jérémy Blanc’s work gives a birational classification of finite Abelian subgroups of the plane Cremona group
\[
\operatorname{Cr}_2(\mathbf C)=\operatorname{Bir}(\mathbf P^2).
\]

The main results can be summarized as follows.

- **Reduction to rational \(G\)-surfaces.** Any finite Abelian subgroup \(G\) can be regularized: after birational conjugacy it acts by automorphisms on a smooth rational surface. Running the \(G\)-equivariant minimal model program reduces the problem to two cases:
  1. \(G\) preserves a conic bundle, hence a pencil of rational curves; or
  2. \(G\) acts minimally on a del Pezzo surface.

- **Classification by fibrations and del Pezzo surfaces.**
  - In the conic-bundle case, the group lies in a de Jonquières-type subgroup. Blanc describes the possible actions on the base and the generic fibre, together with the exceptional involutions that fix hyperelliptic curves.
  - In the del Pezzo case, he analyzes the possible Abelian automorphism groups degree by degree. Most high-degree cases reduce to linear or ruled actions; the genuinely exceptional cases occur on low-degree del Pezzo surfaces and are described explicitly.

- **Abstract group types.** A particularly concise consequence is that every finite Abelian subgroup of \(\operatorname{Cr}_2(\mathbf C)\) is isomorphic to one of
  \[
  \mathbf Z/n\mathbf Z\oplus \mathbf Z/m\mathbf Z,
  \]
  \[
  \mathbf Z/2n\mathbf Z\oplus(\mathbf Z/2\mathbf Z)^2,
  \]
  \[
  (\mathbf Z/4\mathbf Z)^2\oplus\mathbf Z/2\mathbf Z,
  \qquad
  (\mathbf Z/3\mathbf Z)^3,
  \qquad
  (\mathbf Z/2\mathbf Z)^4,
  \]
  with the usual normalization \(n\mid m\) in the first family. Conversely, all these types occur.

  Thus finite Abelian Cremona groups have rank at most \(4\); rank \(4\) occurs only for the elementary \(2\)-group, and the exceptional rank-\(3\) behavior is concentrated at the primes \(2\) and \(3\).

- **Conjugacy is subtler than abstract isomorphism.** Two isomorphic groups need not be conjugate in the Cremona group. Blanc uses fixed curves of positive genus—such as hyperelliptic curves and the curves fixed by Geiser or Bertini involutions—as birational conjugacy invariants. Consequently, some abstract group types occur in families of nonconjugate embeddings.

- **Linearizable versus genuinely Cremona actions.** The work separates groups birationally conjugate to linear actions on \(\mathbf P^2\) from groups whose actions necessarily arise from conic bundles or low-degree del Pezzo surfaces. Fixed positive-genus curves provide a principal obstruction to linearization.

Overall, Blanc’s contribution is not merely a list of possible finite Abelian groups: it describes the geometric models on which they act, identifies the exceptional non-linearizable actions, and explains which invariants distinguish their Cremona-conjugacy classes.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain how to determine whether a finite Abelian subgroup of the plane Cremona group is birationally conjugate to automorphisms of a minimal surface, mentioning any exceptional case.
counterfactuals.output:
Let \(A\subset \operatorname{Cr}_{2}(k)\) be finite Abelian, over an algebraically closed field of characteristic \(0\).

1. **Regularize the action.** Resolve the indeterminacies of all elements of \(A\). This gives a smooth rational surface \(X\) on which \(A\) acts biregularly.

2. **Run the \(A\)-equivariant minimal model program.** Contract \(A\)-orbits of pairwise disjoint \((-1)\)-curves whenever possible. The resulting surface \(S\) is \(A\)-minimal, meaning that there is no further \(A\)-equivariant birational morphism.

3. **Recognize the terminal model.** For a rational surface, one obtains either  
   - a **del Pezzo surface**, with \(\operatorname{rk}\operatorname{Pic}(S)^A=1\), or  
   - an **\(A\)-equivariant conic bundle** \(S\to \mathbf P^{1}\), with \(\operatorname{rk}\operatorname{Pic}(S)^A=2\).

Thus \(A\) is birationally conjugate to a subgroup of \(\operatorname{Aut}(S)\); the practical criterion is that no \(A\)-invariant contractible orbit of exceptional curves remains, equivalently that the invariant Picard group has the appropriate rank above.

If “minimal” means an **ordinary minimal rational surface** such as \(\mathbf P^{2}\) or a Hirzebruch surface, one must be more careful: an \(A\)-minimal surface need not be minimal after forgetting the action. The standard exceptional possibility is an **exceptional conic bundle**, where the singular fibers and distinguished negative sections cannot be contracted \(A\)-equivariantly. Such an action may therefore remain genuinely conic-bundle type rather than descend to automorphisms of \(\mathbf P^{2}\) or a Hirzebruch surface.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a concise mathematical paper abstract describing a linearizability criterion for finite cyclic plane birational groups and classifications involving del Pezzo surfaces and conic bundles.
counterfactuals.output: We study finite cyclic subgroups \(G\subset \operatorname{Bir}(\mathbf P^{2})\) over an algebraically closed field of characteristic \(0\). Using \(G\)-equivariant minimal models, we prove that \(G\) is birationally conjugate to a subgroup of \(\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbf P^{2})\) precisely when no nontrivial element of \(G\) fixes a curve of positive genus. We analyze the two possible minimal models—del Pezzo surfaces and conic bundles—and classify the non-linearizable actions through their fixed-curve data, singular fibers, and induced actions on the Picard lattice. This yields a uniform geometric criterion for linearizability and recovers the exceptional cyclic actions arising from low-degree del Pezzo surfaces and nontrivial conic bundles.
